introduction: Scaling is a hypothesis about a bottleneck. Adding Pods can improve request capacity while exhausting the database connection budget. This lesson connects resource requests, observed saturation and downstream limits.

You will install the Kubernetes resource-metrics API, measure a bounded load, configure an HPA and deliberately provoke an OOM in a separate disposable workload. A small local run establishes mechanics and starting assumptions, not production capacity.
prerequisites: Ubuntu 24.04 Bash in WSL2 or a disposable Linux VM; Docker is running. Use the same terminal unless a step names a second terminal.
Week29 Taskboard/PostgreSQL cluster. Keep the database and its claim. Python3, Docker, kubectl available.

concepts.title: Requests, limits and utilization
paragraphs: A CPU request influences scheduling and provides the denominator for CPU-utilization HPA targets. A CPU limit can throttle; a memory limit can terminate a container that exceeds its enforced memory budget. Neither is the same as measured demand.
concepts.example: With a100m CPU request, usage50m is50% utilization. Raising the request changes that percentage even if work is unchanged.
concepts.judgment: Do not guess a tiny request merely to trigger scaling. Observe steady and peak load, and reserve headroom.

concepts.title: A control loop has prerequisites and consequences
paragraphs: The HPA reads metrics and computes a desired replica count, bounded by min/max and stabilization behavior. Missing metrics or missing requests make the signal unavailable. Metrics Server supplies resource metrics; Prometheus application metrics are a separate system.
Taskboard currently opens short-lived database connections. More replicas or load increase concurrent connections; a future pool needs an explicit per-replica maximum.
concepts.example: If20 replicas each allow10 connections, the potential200 connections may exceed a150-connection database budget before administrators and migrations are counted.
concepts.judgment: Scaling app replicas cannot repair a saturated database or unbounded query. Measure tail latency, errors and dependencies alongside CPU.

steps.title: Install resource metrics in this local cluster
steps.purpose: Download an official versioned release before applying its privileges.

commands.code:
export KUBECONFIG="$HOME/dev-opps-lab/k8s/kubeconfig"
kubectl config current-context
cd "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/k8s"
METRICS_TAG=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"])')
curl -fL "https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/download/$METRICS_TAG/components.yaml" -o metrics-server.yaml
kubectl apply -f metrics-server.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system patch deployment metrics-server --type=json -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'
kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deployment/metrics-server --timeout=180s
kubectl top nodes
kubectl -n devopps top pods
explain: Resolve the official release tag once and retain the downloaded manifest/version. Read its ServiceAccount/RBAC rules before apply: this add-on observes node/workload resource use.

The kind-only insecure-TLS flag accepts the local kubelet serving certificate without validation. This weakens identity verification and must not be carried into production; production needs valid kubelet serving certificates.
top asks the metrics API for current CPU/memory, not historical latency. Initial samples can take a minute.
commands.expected: Numeric CPU/memory values for nodes and Pods.
commands.troubleshoot: If Metrics API is unavailable inspect metrics-server logs and APIService status; do not create HPA evidence from unknown values.

steps.checkpoint: Record metrics version and the local TLS exception with its production alternative.

steps.title: Apply an HPA and generate a bounded load
steps.purpose: Use a small request stream and watch both replicas and database connections.

commands.code:
kubectl -n devopps autoscale deployment taskboard --cpu-percent=60 --min=2 --max=4
kubectl -n devopps get hpa taskboard -w
explain: autoscale creates an HPA targeting60% average CPU utilization of requests, bounded2–4. -w streams changes; stop observation with Ctrl+C.
commands.troubleshoot: If no scale-out occurs that is a valid result: check actual load, CPU request denominator and downstream latency rather than fabricating scaling.

commands.code:
ALICE_TOKEN=$(kubectl -n devopps get secret taskboard-env -o jsonpath='{.data.LAB_ALICE_TOKEN}' | base64 --decode)
kubectl -n devopps run load --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never --command -- sh -c 'i=0; while [ "$i" -lt 120 ]; do wget -T 2 -qO- http://taskboard/livez >/dev/null || echo FAILED; i=$((i+1)); sleep 0.25; done'
kubectl -n devopps top pods
kubectl -n devopps exec postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "SELECT state,count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;"
explain: The Secret read recovers a lab token for independent authenticated testing; base64 is decoding, not decryption. Do not print it.

The health-only load sends120 requests with2-second timeouts at a bounded rate. It isolates platform CPU and is intentionally not a database benchmark. >/dev/null discards successful bodies; failures stay visible.

top measures resources and pg_stat_activity groups database sessions. For representative workload, use the supplied system tests and a separate bounded authenticated task-list stream; record endpoint and concurrency rather than calling health traffic a capacity result.
commands.expected: Completed bounded load; observed metrics and session count. Scale-out may or may not occur.
commands.troubleshoot: No HPA movement under a light workload is expected. A capacity conclusion needs representative traffic and timestamped latency/error measurements.

steps.checkpoint: Record request count, concurrency, elapsed time and whether HPA acted; do not extrapolate a production maximum.

steps.title: Observe the scaling control loop with a bounded CPU experiment
steps.purpose: Separate a controlled autoscaler test from realistic application capacity evidence.

commands.code:
kubectl -n devopps exec deployment/taskboard -- python -c 'import time; end=time.monotonic()+90; n=0
while time.monotonic()<end: n=(n+1)%1000003
print("bounded CPU exercise complete")'
explain: In a separate terminal from the HPA watch, run a 90-second CPU loop inside one disposable app container. It deliberately consumes CPU measured by the autoscaler; it is not a business request benchmark.
The time.monotonic deadline bounds the load. The existing HPA may raise replicas toward its maximum of four; new replicas dilute average utilization and the load ends automatically.
commands.expected: Observe HPA utilization, desired replicas and new Pods. After load ends, record when scale-down occurs; default stabilization can retain replicas for several minutes.
commands.troubleshoot: If metrics are unknown, inspect Metrics Server. If scaling is delayed, inspect HPA conditions and CPU requests; do not remove bounds or claim the experiment proves production throughput.

commands.code:
kubectl -n devopps describe hpa taskboard
kubectl -n devopps get pods
kubectl -n devopps exec postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "SELECT state,count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;"
explain: Describe HPA decisions and inspect replica and database connection counts. Existing requests and their configured resources determine the computed utilization.
commands.expected: Evidence separates load, metric, scale-out and eventual scale-in timestamps.
commands.troubleshoot: If no scale occurs, report the condition and actual measurements rather than inventing a result.

steps.checkpoint: Explain why this proves a control-loop response but not the number of user requests the application can safely serve.

steps.title: Measure latency distribution
steps.purpose: Port-forward Service in a second terminal as week29; run this bounded measurement in the first.

commands.code:
mkdir -p "$HOME/dev-opps-lab/evidence/w30"
export ALICE_TOKEN
python3 - <<'PY'
import concurrent.futures,json,os,time,urllib.request,urllib.error
url='http://127.0.0.1:18000/tasks'
def one(_):
 start=time.perf_counter()
 req=urllib.request.Request(url,headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+os.environ['ALICE_TOKEN']})
 try:
  with urllib.request.urlopen(req,timeout=3) as r: r.read(); ok=r.status==200
 except (urllib.error.URLError,TimeoutError): ok=False
 return time.perf_counter()-start,ok
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool: rows=list(pool.map(one,range(100)))
times=sorted(t for t,ok in rows)
print(json.dumps({'requests':100,'concurrency':4,'errors':sum(not ok for t,ok in rows),'p50_ms':times[49]*1000,'p95_ms':times[94]*1000,'max_ms':times[-1]*1000},indent=2))
PY
explain: The standard-library script sends100 authenticated list requests with4 workers and a3-second timeout. It counts failures and computes rank-based sample percentiles; reading each response includes body transfer time. export makes the token available to this child process.
commands.expected: JSON with100requests, errors and p50/p95/max in milliseconds.
commands.troubleshoot: Port-forward tests one selected Pod and includes tunnel overhead; it is useful for this bounded measurement, not proof of load-balanced fleet throughput. Check the tunnel if every request fails.

steps.checkpoint: Write a capacity assumption with an observed range and a falsification test.

failure.title: Separate OOM from health-check failure
failure.boundary: A new memory-hog Pod only; do not reduce PostgreSQL memory.

inject.code: kubectl -n devopps run memory-hog --image=python:3.14-slim --restart=Never --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"memory-hog","image":"python:3.14-slim","command":["python","-c","a=bytearray(256*1024*1024); import time; time.sleep(60)"],"resources":{"requests":{"memory":"16Mi"},"limits":{"memory":"48Mi"}}}]}}'
explain: The process allocates256MiB inside a48Mi memory limit. The Pod is isolated and has no probes or persistent data.
inject.troubleshoot: An image-pull error must be resolved before this fault is actually exercised.

investigate.code:
kubectl -n devopps get pod memory-hog -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].state.terminated}'
kubectl -n devopps describe pod memory-hog
explain: Read the explicit termination reason and events.
investigate.expected: OOMKilled, often exit137; there is no liveness probe.
investigate.troubleshoot: Exit137 alone is insufficient because other SIGKILL causes exist; require the OOMKilled reason.

hints: Which field identifies the termination reason?

explanation: The memory controller killed the process for exceeding its budget. A liveness restart is a different mechanism and should show probe failures. Repair memory demand or justified sizing, not probe timing.

recover.troubleshoot: Do not change node memory settings for this bounded experiment.

verification.code:
kubectl -n devopps get deployment taskboard
kubectl -n devopps top pods
explain: Check healthy service replicas and measured memory.
verification.expected: Healthy service unaffected; no memory-hog Pod.
verification.troubleshoot: Look at actual Ready counts, not only desired HPA replicas.

questions.prompt: What happens if CPU requests are absent?
questions.answer: The utilization target lacks its denominator; the HPA cannot derive that metric correctly. Inspect HPA conditions rather than assuming it is active.
More Pods can open more sessions and saturate a shared database; enforce a total connection/capacity budget and bound maximum replicas.

questions.prompt: Why report p95 and failures together?
questions.answer: A service can fail quickly and look fast. Tail latency describes slow requests while error ratio prevents a fast failure from being interpreted as a good experience.

exercise.brief: Choose starting resource and replica budgets from your measurements.
constraints: Keep max replicas4 in this local lab.
hints: A missing metric is a finding, not zero utilization.
solution: Compare idle and loaded readings, reserve headroom and compute maximum app-side connections. Propose a representative next experiment instead of presenting the laptop maximum as production capacity.

cleanup.code:
kubectl -n devopps delete pod load --ignore-not-found
kubectl -n devopps delete hpa taskboard
kubectl -n devopps scale deployment/taskboard --replicas=2
explain: Remove temporary load and the HPA before later declarative replica experiments. Restore2replicas; keep resource metrics for observation.
cleanup.expected: 2replicas and no HPA controlling the field.
cleanup.troubleshoot: Deleting the HPA avoids two owners competing over replicas in the GitOps lesson.

repoConnections.principle: Reliability is measured against a useful user action.
repoConnections.application: Keep errors and latency together and state what the health-only load leaves untested.

repoConnections.principle: An extension needs a clear operational purpose.
repoConnections.application: Metrics Server is added for HPA resource metrics; document its permissions and certificate exception instead of installing an entire monitoring suite by habit.

notes: No Kubernetes load or OOM run was executed on the authoring host. Capture actual values; none are supplied as fabricated results.
title: Measure capacity before scaling
outcome: Set resource requests and limits from observed behavior and reason about autoscaling.
